title: Local or international museum collections
prompt:
Some people believe that museums and galleries should focus mainly on the history and art of their own country. Others think they should display objects and artworks from all over the world.

Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
tips: Give each view its own body paragraph and explain it fairly, even if you disagree with it.
Your opinion must appear clearly: state it in the introduction and confirm it in the conclusion, or give it a separate paragraph.
Use reporting language to show whose view you are describing ('Supporters of this view argue...', 'Those on the other side contend...').

samples.text:
Museums and galleries are important places in every country. Some people think they should show only their own country's history and art, but other people think they should show things from all countries. In this essay I will discuss both views and give my opinion.

On the one hand, some people believe that museums should focus on their own country. This is because people, especially children, need to learn about their history and culture. If they visit a museum about their country, they will understand where they come from and they will be proud of their country. Also, many tourists come to a country because they want to see the local culture, not things from other countries.

On the other hand, other people think museums should have things from all over the world. This is because not everyone can travel to other countries, so museums give them a chance to see art from different cultures. For example, in my country there is a museum with Japanese and Chinese art and many students visit it. This helps people to understand other cultures and be more open-minded.

In my opinion, I think museums should show both. Local history is important but international art is also important because the world is more connected now. Museums can have a big section for local history and a smaller section for international art. In this way, everyone can be satisfied.

In conclusion, both views have good points. I believe the best is to show both local and international objects in museums.
samples.commentary: Task Response: both views are discussed and an opinion is given, but ideas are developed only in general terms and the writer's own position is underdeveloped, with little explanation of why a balance is best. Coherence and Cohesion: the structure is clear, but the cohesive devices are mechanical ('On the one hand', 'Also', 'This is because' repeated), and 'In my opinion, I think' is redundant. Lexical Resource: adequate but limited and repetitive ('important', 'show', 'things'), with few topic-specific words. Grammatical Range and Accuracy: mostly accurate simple and complex sentences, though the range is limited and there are slips like 'the best is to show'. Band 6.

samples.text:
Museums play a key role in shaping how people understand both their own society and the wider world. While some argue that they should concentrate on national history and art, others believe their collections should be global. In my view, the most valuable museums combine the two.

Those who favour a national focus argue that museums are the main guardians of a country's heritage. Objects such as traditional textiles, manuscripts and tools tell the story of how a nation developed, and if local museums do not preserve and display them, nobody else will. This is particularly important for younger generations, who are surrounded by global media and may otherwise lose touch with their own traditions. Furthermore, visitors from abroad often seek out exactly this kind of local material.

On the other hand, supporters of international collections point out that most people will never travel widely, so a museum may be their only opportunity to see Egyptian sculpture or West African masks. Exposure to other cultures can broaden people's perspectives and encourage tolerance. Global collections also highlight connections between civilisations, such as the trade routes that carried ideas and goods between Asia and Europe.

Personally, I believe that these aims are not in conflict. A museum can place its own history at the centre while also showing how it relates to the rest of the world. For example, an exhibition on a country's spice trade could display local artefacts alongside objects from the places it traded with, giving visitors a richer understanding of both.

In conclusion, although there are strong arguments for each approach, I think museums serve the public best when they present national heritage within a global context.
samples.commentary: Task Response: both views are presented clearly and supported with relevant ideas, and the writer's opinion is clear and explained, though some support remains generalised. Coherence and Cohesion: logical organisation with a clear progression from each view to the writer's own position; a good range of cohesive devices is used appropriately. Lexical Resource: a good range of vocabulary ('guardians of a country's heritage', 'lose touch with', 'broaden people's perspectives', 'artefacts'), used accurately. Grammatical Range and Accuracy: a variety of complex structures, including relative clauses, conditionals and participle phrases, with good control. The final example is useful but brief, which keeps this at band 7.

samples.text:
Whether museums should look inward, to the history and art of their own nation, or outward, to the achievements of humanity as a whole, is a question about what we want such institutions to do. Although both positions have merit, I would argue that the most meaningful museums refuse to choose between them.

The case for a national focus rests on the idea of custodianship. Every country possesses objects, from folk costumes to archival photographs, whose significance is primarily local and which would almost certainly be neglected if domestic institutions did not prioritise them. For citizens, encountering these items can create a tangible sense of continuity with the past, something that is arguably more needed than ever in an age when popular culture is increasingly homogenised. There is also an economic dimension, since tourists rarely cross the world to see what they could see at home.

Advocates of international collections, however, see museums as windows rather than mirrors. For the many people who cannot afford to travel, a gallery of Persian ceramics or Andean textiles may be their only direct contact with distant cultures, and such encounters can challenge stereotypes in a way that books and screens rarely do. A global perspective also reveals that no national culture developed in isolation; much of what a country regards as its own was shaped by trade, migration and exchange.

It is this last point that leads me to favour a synthesis. A museum that tells its nation's story honestly will inevitably have to show the foreign influences woven through it. A display of local pottery, for instance, becomes far more illuminating when placed beside the imported pieces that inspired it.

In short, national heritage and world culture are best understood together, and museums should be designed to reflect that relationship.
samples.commentary: Task Response: both views are explored in depth with well-chosen, specific support, and the writer's position develops logically out of the discussion rather than simply being stated. Coherence and Cohesion: ideas are sequenced skilfully and paragraphs are linked through conceptual cohesion ('It is this last point that leads me...'), with no reliance on formulaic connectors. Lexical Resource: sophisticated and precise vocabulary ('custodianship', 'homogenised', 'windows rather than mirrors', 'synthesis', 'woven through it'), used naturally. Grammatical Range and Accuracy: a wide range of structures, including cleft sentences, 'whose' relative clauses and fronted clauses, with full flexibility and accuracy. Band 8.
